parentTitle: The Older Person, Multimorbidity & Cancer Care
title: Oncology emergencies: MSCC and others
blurb: Recognise metastatic spinal cord compression early, act on NICE NG234's time frames, and spot hypercalcaemia and other cancer emergencies.
question: Mr Reid, 68, has metastatic prostate cancer. He tells the ward nurse that his mid-back pain has been worsening for a week, it wakes him at night, and today his legs feel heavy and he is unsteady walking. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

teach.h: What metastatic spinal cord compression is
teach.body: Metastatic spinal cord compression (MSCC) happens when cancer that has spread to the spine presses on the spinal cord or cauda equina, by tumour growth or vertebral collapse. Without fast treatment it can cause permanent paralysis and loss of bladder and bowel control. NICE NG234 treats suspected MSCC with neurological symptoms as an oncological emergency. Plain English: in anyone with cancer, new back pain is a warning, and new leg weakness, numbness or bladder or bowel change is an emergency.

rows.label: Character
values: Severe unremitting or progressive back pain

rows.label: Triggers
values: Mechanical; worse on coughing, sneezing, straining

rows.label: Other
values: Night pain disturbing sleep; local tenderness; claudication
Bladder or bowel dysfunction; radicular pain

steps.sub: Oral (or parenteral equivalent) as soon as possible

steps.sub: As soon as possible, always within 24 h

items.label: MRI for suspected spinal metastases without MSCC
urgent radiotherapy if not for surgery

teach.text: A plain spinal X-ray does NOT rule out spinal metastases or MSCC: NICE says do not use it. And do not wait for leg weakness: in someone with cancer, pain with the box 1 features already needs advice from the MSCC coordinator within 24 hours.

teach.h: Nursing care while immobilised and on steroids
items: Nurse supine (flat or partial elevation) to minimise spinal weight bearing; adjust if pain or breathlessness.
Seek expert advice on spinal stability within 24 hours to shorten immobilisation.
Give pain relief promptly, including while waiting for scans; review after changes.
On corticosteroids: monitor blood glucose and offer a proton pump inhibitor.
If MSCC and spinal metastases are ruled out after an early dose, dexamethasone is stopped.
After surgery or the start of radiotherapy, dexamethasone is reduced gradually until stopped.

teach.body: When assessment suggests the spine is likely to be stable, start graded sitting followed by weight bearing, monitoring neurological symptoms and pain continuously. Continue to unsupported sitting and walking if there is no orthostatic hypotension, no significant increase in pain and no neurological deterioration. If pain or neurological symptoms increase significantly, return the person to a position where the changes reverse and reassess spinal stability. Mobilise even if surgery or radiotherapy is not appropriate.

teach.h: Scenario: Mr Reid on the oncology ward
teach.body: Mr Reid, 68, has metastatic prostate cancer. His mid-back pain has worsened for a week and wakes him at night; today his legs feel heavy and he is unsteady. The nurse recognises cord compression symptoms, contacts the MSCC coordinator immediately, keeps him lying flat on bed rest, and gives analgesia promptly. Dexamethasone 16 mg is given as prescribed, with blood glucose monitoring and a PPI, and a whole-spine MRI is arranged within 24 hours.

teach.caption: Recognition level only for hypercalcaemia, SVCO and tumour lysis (no current NICE guideline); follow local acute oncology protocols.

items: Cancer + cord compression symptoms: contact the MSCC coordinator immediately; treat as an emergency.
Cancer + spinal pain features only: advice through the coordinator within 24 hours.
MRI within 24 hours for suspected MSCC; within 1 week for suspected spinal metastases; no plain X-ray.
Dexamethasone 16 mg as soon as possible for neurological signs; monitor glucose, give a PPI.
Nurse supine if immobilised; graded sitting when the spine is likely stable.

summary: You can now recognise the warning features of spinal metastases and MSCC and act on NICE NG234's time frames for referral, imaging, dexamethasone and positioning. You can also recognise hypercalcaemia and other oncology emergencies that need urgent escalation.

A.q: Four people with a history of cancer report new symptoms. For which person does NICE NG234 say the MSCC coordinator should be contacted IMMEDIATELY?
options: Mrs Tate, with back pain that is worse on coughing
Mr Ives, with new numbness in both legs
Mr Shah, with back pain waking him at night
Ms Bell, with localised tenderness over the spine
A.why: NG234 rec 1.3.2: immediately contact the MSCC coordinator if a person with cancer presents with symptoms or signs of cord compression, such as numbness or sensory loss. Treat it as an oncological emergency.

whyNot.0: Pain worse on straining suggests spinal metastases; advice via the coordinator is within 24 hours.
whyNot.2: Night pain suggests spinal metastases; advice via the coordinator is within 24 hours.
whyNot.3: Localised tenderness is a pain feature; advice via the coordinator is within 24 hours.

A.q: Mrs Sharp had breast cancer 5 years ago and now has progressive thoracic back pain with no neurological symptoms. The MSCC coordinator suspects spinal metastases without MSCC. Within what time does NICE NG234 say an MRI should be done?
options: Within 24 hours
Within 48 hours
Within 2 weeks
Within 1 week
A.why: NG234 rec 1.5.3: offer an MRI within 1 week, at the local hospital, for clinical suspicion of spinal metastases without suspicion of MSCC.

whyNot.0: Within 24 hours applies to suspected MSCC with neurological symptoms.
whyNot.1: 48 hours is not an NG234 time frame.
whyNot.2: 2 weeks is longer than NICE allows.

A.q: A GP plans a plain X-ray of the spine for Mr Ford, who has lung cancer and new severe back pain, to rule out spinal metastases. What does NICE NG234 say?
options: Do not use plain X-ray to diagnose or rule them out
Use plain X-ray first, then MRI if it is abnormal
Use plain X-ray if MRI is not available within a week
Use plain X-ray with CT to rule out cord compression
A.why: NG234 rec 1.5.9: do not do a plain X-ray of the spine to diagnose or rule out spinal metastases or MSCC. MRI is the investigation; CT if MRI is contraindicated.

whyNot.1: A normal X-ray can miss metastases, so NICE does not use it as a first step.
whyNot.2: If MRI is contraindicated the alternative is CT, not plain X-ray.
whyNot.3: Plain X-ray has no role in diagnosing or excluding MSCC.

B.q: Mrs Lowe was given dexamethasone 16 mg for suspected MSCC before her MRI. The MRI shows no spinal metastases and no cord compression. What does NICE NG234 advise about the dexamethasone?
options: Reduce it gradually over 2 weeks
Continue 16 mg daily until oncology review
Continue 8 mg daily as prevention
Discontinue it
B.why: NG234 rec 1.8.2: if dexamethasone is given before imaging and spinal metastases and MSCC are ruled out, discontinue it. The course has been short, so it can be stopped.

whyNot.0: Gradual reduction applies after surgery or radiotherapy for confirmed MSCC, not when it is ruled out.
whyNot.1: Continuing serves no purpose once MSCC is excluded and risks side effects.
whyNot.2: NICE does not recommend preventive steroids once MSCC is ruled out.

B.q: Mr Reid is taking dexamethasone 16 mg daily while awaiting radiotherapy for MSCC. Which additional care does NICE NG234 recommend while he takes corticosteroids?
options: Daily weights and a fluid restriction
Weekly thyroid function tests
Blood glucose monitoring and a PPI
INR checks and stopping his LMWH
B.why: NG234 rec 1.8.8: for people taking corticosteroids, monitor blood glucose and offer proton pump inhibitor acid suppression.

whyNot.0: Weights and fluid restriction are not the NG234 steroid recommendations.
whyNot.1: Thyroid tests are not part of NG234 steroid monitoring.
whyNot.3: INR and LMWH changes are not linked to corticosteroid use in NG234.

B.q: Mr Ford, 70, has lung cancer. Over 4 days he has become very thirsty, passes large amounts of urine, is constipated and is newly confused. What should the nurse suspect and do?
options: Opioid side effects: give a laxative and review his bowels in 3 days
Possible hypercalcaemia: escalate for an urgent calcium level
Dehydration: encourage oral fluids and recheck tomorrow
Brain metastases: request a routine outpatient scan
B.why: Thirst, polyuria, constipation and confusion together in a person with cancer suggest hypercalcaemia of malignancy, which needs urgent escalation and a calcium level.

whyNot.0: Opioids cause constipation but not thirst and polyuria; this pattern needs urgent blood tests.
whyNot.2: Dehydration is part of the picture, but the cause needs urgent investigation, not a day's wait.
whyNot.3: New confusion needs urgent assessment, and the full pattern points to hypercalcaemia.

C.q: Mr Reid, 68, has metastatic prostate cancer. His mid-back pain has worsened for a week and wakes him at night. Today his legs feel heavy and he is unsteady walking. Which plan follows NICE NG234?
options: Contact the MSCC coordinator now, nurse flat, dexamethasone 16 mg, MRI within 24 h
Request a spinal X-ray, mobilise with the physiotherapist and review his analgesia
Seek advice from the MSCC coordinator within 24 h and book an MRI within 1 week
Give analgesia, review at the next ward round and book an MRI within 1 week
C.why: Gait disturbance and limb weakness are cord compression symptoms: contact the MSCC coordinator immediately (1.3.2), immobilise and nurse supine if instability is suggested (1.4.1, 1.4.3), give dexamethasone 16 mg as soon as possible (1.8.1) and MRI within 24 hours (1.5.2).

whyNot.1: Plain X-ray is not used, and mobilising before stability is assessed risks harm.
whyNot.2: The 24-hour advice and 1-week MRI are for pain without cord compression signs; he has neurological symptoms.
whyNot.3: Waiting for a ward round delays an oncological emergency.

C.q: Four people have MSCC that is not suitable for spinal surgery. For which person does NICE NG234 recommend urgent radiotherapy within 24 hours?
options: Mr Ali, complete paraplegia for 3 weeks, with pain well controlled
Mrs Nye, overall prognosis considered poor by the team
Ms Hart, new leg weakness, otherwise well and mobile last week
Mr Cole, spinal metastases with no symptoms on imaging
C.why: NG234 rec 1.10.4: offer urgent radiotherapy (as soon as possible and within 24 hours) to people with MSCC not suitable for surgery, unless they have had complete tetraplegia or paraplegia for 2 weeks or more with well-controlled pain, or a poor overall prognosis.

whyNot.0: Complete paraplegia for 2 weeks or more with controlled pain is an exception to urgent radiotherapy.
whyNot.1: A poor overall prognosis is an exception to urgent radiotherapy.
whyNot.3: Asymptomatic spinal metastases are not MSCC and are not in this urgent group.

C.q: Mr Wu, 60, has no cancer diagnosis. He has lost weight and has had 6 weeks of progressive thoracic back pain that wakes him at night. He has no neurological symptoms. Cancer is suspected. What does NICE NG234 recommend?
options: Contact the MSCC coordinator immediately as an emergency
Refer him for urgent oncology assessment
Refer him to physiotherapy for mechanical back pain
Review him again in 6 weeks if the pain persists
C.why: NG234 rec 1.3.5: if a person without a past or current cancer diagnosis has box 1 pain features and cancer is suspected, refer for urgent oncology assessment.

whyNot.0: Immediate coordinator contact is for people with a cancer diagnosis and cord compression signs.
whyNot.2: Night pain, progression and weight loss are red flags, not simple mechanical pain.
whyNot.3: Delay is unsafe when cancer is suspected.

reteach.title: Back pain plus cancer: think spine first
reteach.question: What turns 'back pain' into an emergency in someone with cancer?

blocks.h: Pain is the warning; neurology is the alarm
blocks.body: Spinal metastases usually announce themselves with pain that is progressive, unremitting, worse at night or on straining. That needs advice through the MSCC coordinator within 24 hours. Once the cord is being squeezed, neurological symptoms appear: weakness, unsteadiness, numbness, bladder or bowel change. That is an emergency: contact the coordinator immediately, give dexamethasone and get an MRI within 24 hours.

bands.label: Cancer + low back pain, no evidence: safety-net advice
Cancer + pain features: coordinator within 24 h, MRI within 1 week
Cancer + neurological signs: coordinator NOW, MRI within 24 h

blocks.text: No plain X-ray. MRI (or CT if MRI is contraindicated) is the scan.

explain.body: In someone with cancer, cord compression symptoms (bladder or bowel dysfunction, gait disturbance, limb weakness, numbness, radicular pain) mean contacting the MSCC coordinator immediately. Pain features alone (progressive, unremitting, night pain, worse on straining, tenderness, claudication) mean advice via the coordinator within 24 hours.

test.q: Ms Kent had bowel cancer 3 years ago. She now has 3 weeks of progressive back pain that wakes her at night, with no neurological symptoms. What does NICE NG234 advise?
options: Seek advice through the MSCC coordinator within 24 hours
Contact the MSCC coordinator immediately as an emergency
Give analgesia and review in 4 weeks
Request a plain spinal X-ray first
test.why: NG234 rec 1.3.3: with a cancer history and pain suggesting spinal metastases, seek advice through the MSCC coordinator within 24 hours.

whyNot.1: Immediate contact is for cord compression symptoms or signs; she has none.
whyNot.2: A 4-week wait ignores red-flag pain in someone with cancer.
whyNot.3: NICE says do not use plain X-ray to diagnose or rule out spinal metastases.

explain.body: Suspected MSCC: MRI as soon as possible and always within 24 hours, locally if possible. Suspected spinal metastases without MSCC: MRI within 1 week. Whole-spine sequences. CT if MRI is contraindicated. No plain X-ray.

test.q: Mrs Gill has lung cancer and new weakness in both legs. Within what time does NICE NG234 say she should have an MRI scan?
options: Within 1 week
Within 48 hours
Within 4 hours
Within 24 hours
test.why: NG234 rec 1.5.2: offer an MRI to people with suspected MSCC as soon as possible and always within 24 hours.

whyNot.0: One week is for suspected spinal metastases without MSCC.
whyNot.1: 48 hours is longer than the NICE standard.
whyNot.2: 4 hours is not the NG234 standard; it is as soon as possible and within 24 hours.

explain.body: Immobilise without delay (including for transfer) if there are neurological symptoms or signs suggesting spinal instability; consider it for moderate to severe movement-related pain. Nurse supine, flat or with partial elevation; adjust if pain or breathlessness. Get expert advice on stability within 24 hours.

test.q: Mr Hayes has suspected MSCC with neurological signs suggesting spinal instability. How does NICE NG234 say he should be positioned?
options: Sitting upright in a chair to aid breathing
Supine, lying flat or with partial elevation
Prone, to take pressure off the spine
Side-lying with the head of the bed at 45 degrees
test.why: NG234 rec 1.4.3: nurse people who are immobilised in a supine position (lying flat or with partial elevation) to minimise weight bearing by the spine.

whyNot.0: Sitting upright loads the spine; it is for after stability is confirmed.
whyNot.2: Prone positioning is not the NG234 recommendation.
whyNot.3: Head elevation to 45 degrees increases spinal loading; NICE says flat or partial elevation.

explain.body: For neurological symptoms or signs of MSCC, give 16 mg oral dexamethasone (or parenteral equivalent) as soon as possible, then daily until surgery or radiotherapy, then reduce gradually. Monitor glucose and give a PPI. Also recognise hypercalcaemia (thirst, polyuria, constipation, confusion) and neutropenic sepsis.

test.q: What dose of dexamethasone does NICE NG234 recommend as soon as possible for a person with neurological symptoms of MSCC?
options: 4 mg orally
8 mg orally
16 mg orally
32 mg orally
test.why: NG234 rec 1.8.1: offer 16 mg of oral dexamethasone (or equivalent parenteral dose) as soon as possible.

whyNot.0: 4 mg is below the NICE dose.
whyNot.1: 8 mg is below the NICE dose.
whyNot.3: 32 mg is double the NICE dose.
